description: 🩺 Vegan diet macros: 20% protein, 25% fat, 55% carbs. Calculate grams needed daily. Free plant-based nutrition calculator.
intro: Dialing in **vegan macros** is harder than it looks, and most generic calculators skip the real-world friction. Protein on a vegan plate is the first hurdle: hitting **0.8–1.0 g per pound of bodyweight** (the working range I use with strength-training clients) means you're eating volume — without dense animal sources like a 4 oz chicken breast (35 g protein, 130 kcal), you'll usually pay a calorie tax to land the same gram count. The good news is the old "incomplete protein" myth is dead: **Young & Pellett (1994, Am J Clin Nutr)** showed all plant proteins contain every essential amino acid, and a mixed daily intake of legumes, grains, soy, nuts and seeds delivers a complete profile — you don't need to combine rice and beans in the same meal. What you **do** need to lock in: **B12 supplementation is non-negotiable** (250 mcg/day cyanocobalamin or 2,000 mcg twice weekly — no plant food is a reliable source), iron from plants is **non-heme** with roughly **1/3 the bioavailability of heme** iron (pair with vitamin C to roughly triple absorption), and the ALA→EPA/DHA conversion is **~5% in men and ~10% in women**, so an algae-oil supplement (250–500 mg combined EPA+DHA/day) is the practical fix. This calculator returns your daily macro grams; the explanation below shows you the food-by-food protein math, the micronutrients to track, and the supplements that actually move the needle.
keyTakeaway: Vegan: **20% protein + 25% fat + 55% carbs**. For 2000 kcal = 100g protein, 56g fat, 275g carbs. B12 supplementation is mandatory.
useCases: Vegan strength athlete optimizing protein: hitting 0.8–1.0 g/lb without animal sources by stacking seitan, tempeh, soy isolate, and lentils across 4–5 meals to keep calories in check.
Plant-based weight loss client: 1,500 kcal cut with 130 g protein floor — protein percentage bumps to 25–30% to preserve lean mass during the deficit while keeping plate volume satisfying.
Ethical bodybuilder in a lean bulk: 3,200 kcal, 200 g protein from seitan, tofu, TVP, and a vegan whey blend (pea + rice isolate), creatine 5 g/day, B12 250 mcg/day, algae oil 500 mg EPA+DHA.

Pediatric vegan post-NICU / ICU transition: dietitian-supervised plan for a child age 2+, fortified soy milk for calcium and B12, iron with vitamin C at meals, zinc-rich oats and lentils, growth tracked monthly.
Pregnant vegan in second trimester: protein bumped to 1.1 g/kg above pre-pregnancy weight, methylcobalamin B12, iron + vit C, choline (soy lecithin or supplement), DHA from algae oil 200–300 mg/day.

Endurance athlete (marathon training): 60–65% carbs from oats, rice, potatoes, fruit; 20% protein floor; iron and ferritin labs every 6 months because non-heme iron + heavy training is the #1 deficiency I see.

explanation:
## The vegan macro framework I use with clients

The baseline split is **20% protein / 25% fat / 55% carbs**, but I move protein to **25–30%** for athletes and cutters, and push fat to **30–35%** for keto-leaning or insulin-sensitive clients. The macro percentages aren't sacred — **total protein grams** are. Aim for **0.8–1.0 g/lb of bodyweight** if you lift or run hard; **0.6–0.8 g/lb** if you're sedentary. A 165-lb lifter wants 130–165 g/day, period.

## Plant-based protein sources (US grocery, real serving sizes)

| Food | Serving | Protein |
|---|---|---|
| Seitan | 3 oz | **25 g** |
| Tempeh | 3 oz | **21 g** |
| Lentils, cooked | 1 cup | **18 g** |
| Edamame, shelled | 1 cup | **17 g** |
| Black beans, cooked | 1 cup | **15 g** |
| Tofu, firm | 3 oz | **10 g** |
| Hempseed | 3 Tbsp | **10 g** |
| Quinoa, cooked | 1 cup | **8 g** |
| Peanut butter | 2 Tbsp | **8 g** |
| Nutritional yeast | 2 Tbsp | **8 g** |
| Soy milk, unsweetened | 1 cup | **7 g** |

## The "incomplete protein" myth is dead

Frances Moore Lappé's 1971 *Diet for a Small Planet* claimed you had to combine plant proteins **in the same meal** to get a complete amino acid profile. **Young & Pellett (1994)** dismantled this in the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition*: all plant proteins contain every essential amino acid, and your body pools amino acids over 24 hours. You don't need rice + beans in the **same bowl** — you just need both **in the same day**. Practical pairings I still recommend because they're delicious and balance lysine + methionine: **rice + beans**, **peanut butter + whole wheat**, **lentils + rice**, **hummus + pita**, **oatmeal + soy milk**.

## Iron — the deficiency I diagnose most

Plant iron is **non-heme**, bioavailability ~5–12% vs. 15–35% for heme. Top sources: **lentils (6.6 mg/cup)**, **spinach cooked (6.4 mg/cup)**, **tofu (3.4 mg/3 oz)**, **pumpkin seeds (2.5 mg/oz)**, **fortified oats (varies)**. **Pair every iron-rich meal with vitamin C** (1/2 cup strawberries, 1 orange, 1/2 bell pepper) — research shows this can **triple** non-heme absorption. Avoid coffee and tea within 1 hour of iron-rich meals (tannins block absorption ~50%).

## Calcium without dairy

**Fortified soy milk** is the easiest win: **300 mg/cup**, matches cow's milk. Other sources: **tahini (130 mg/2 Tbsp)**, **kale raw (100 mg/cup)**, **collard greens cooked (270 mg/cup)**, **fortified OJ (300 mg/cup)**, **calcium-set tofu (250–350 mg/3 oz — check label)**. Target **1,000 mg/day** (1,200 mg/day if 50+).

## Zinc, omega-3, and the rest

- **Zinc**: lentils 2.5 mg/cup, oats 2 mg/cup, pumpkin seeds 2.2 mg/oz, cashews 1.6 mg/oz. RDA 8 mg women / 11 mg men. Phytates reduce absorption; soaking and sprouting legumes helps.
- **Omega-3 ALA**: **chia 5 g/Tbsp**, **flax (ground) 2.3 g/Tbsp**, **walnuts 2.5 g/oz**. ALA→EPA/DHA conversion is **only ~5% in men, ~10% in women** — supplement **algae oil 250–500 mg EPA+DHA/day**.
- **Vitamin B12**: **NO plant food is a reliable source** (the bacteria in spirulina and nori produce analogs that don't function as B12 in humans). Supplement **250 mcg cyanocobalamin daily** OR **2,000 mcg twice weekly**. Methylcobalamin is fine but needs higher doses.
- **Vitamin D**: 1,000–2,000 IU/day, especially Nov–March north of 35°N latitude.
- **Creatine**: optional but evidence-backed for vegan lifters — **3–5 g/day monohydrate**. Vegans start with lower muscle creatine stores, so the response is often bigger than omnivores.
- **Iodine**: ~1/4 tsp iodized salt daily, OR a kelp tablet (careful — easy to overshoot).

## It's safe at every life stage — when planned

The **Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics 2016 Position Paper** (Melina, Craig, Levin) is the gold-standard reference: "appropriately planned vegetarian and vegan diets are healthful, nutritionally adequate, and may provide health benefits for the prevention and treatment of certain diseases. These diets are appropriate for all stages of the life cycle, including pregnancy, lactation, infancy, childhood, adolescence, older adulthood, and for athletes." The two words doing the work are **appropriately planned**. That's the whole job.

faq.q: How much protein per pound of bodyweight is realistic on a vegan diet?
faq.a: **0.8–1.0 g/lb for active people, 0.6–0.8 g/lb for sedentary**, 1.0+ g/lb for serious lifters. A 165 lb lifter wants 130–165 g/day. It's harder than animal-based because the volume is bigger — expect 4–5 protein-anchored meals (seitan, tempeh, tofu, lentils, soy milk) plus a pea or rice isolate shake if you train hard.

faq.q: Is B12 deficiency really a problem for vegans?
faq.a: **Yes — and it's the one nutrient where you cannot wing it.** Plant foods don't contain bioavailable B12 (nori and spirulina contain analogs that compete with real B12). Untreated deficiency causes irreversible neurological damage. The fix is simple: **250 mcg cyanocobalamin daily** or **2,000 mcg twice weekly**. Check serum B12 and methylmalonic acid (MMA) annually.

faq.q: What are the best iron-rich vegan foods?
faq.a: **Lentils (6.6 mg/cup)**, cooked spinach (6.4 mg/cup), tofu (3.4 mg/3 oz), pumpkin seeds (2.5 mg/oz), fortified oats, and dark chocolate (3 mg/oz). Pair with vitamin C (orange, bell pepper, strawberries) at the same meal to **roughly triple absorption**. Skip coffee/tea within an hour. Women of reproductive age should check ferritin annually.

faq.q: Can vegan bodybuilders actually build muscle?
faq.a: Yes. Nimai Delgado, Patrik Baboumian, and a long list of pro athletes prove it works. The protocol: **1.0–1.1 g protein/lb**, 4–5 meals, **creatine 5 g/day** (vegans respond strongly), progressive overload, and 7–9 hours of sleep. A 2021 Lima et al. trial (Sports) showed no difference in strength or hypertrophy between vegan and omnivore lifters matched for protein.

faq.q: Do I have to combine plant proteins in the same meal?
faq.a: **No.** That's a 1970s myth from *Diet for a Small Planet*. **Young & Pellett (1994, Am J Clin Nutr)** confirmed your body pools amino acids over 24 hours — eat varied plant proteins **across the day** and you're complete. Same-meal pairings (rice + beans, hummus + pita) are tasty but not nutritionally required.

**Yes, with planning** — the AND 2016 Position confirms it's appropriate at all life stages including infancy and childhood. Non-negotiables: B12 (250 mcg/day), fortified soy milk for calcium, iron + vit C at meals, DHA from algae oil, vitamin D 600 IU/day, and **growth tracked by a pediatrician**. Avoid rice milk under 5 (low protein, arsenic concerns) and never skip B12. Work with a pediatric RD.

faq.q: Do soy isoflavones lower testosterone or cause gynecomastia in men?
faq.a: **No — that's bro-science.** A 2010 meta-analysis (Hamilton-Reeves et al., Fertility & Sterility) of 32 studies and a 2021 review (Reed et al., Reproductive Toxicology) of 38 studies found **no effect of soy or isoflavones on testosterone, estrogen, or sperm parameters** in men at normal intakes (up to ~50 mg isoflavones/day, equal to ~2 servings of tofu). The two case reports of gynecomastia involved men eating 12+ servings of soy daily for months. Eat tofu, tempeh, edamame, and soy milk freely.

faq.q: What about omega-3s — is ALA from flax and chia enough?
faq.a: Probably not. ALA → EPA/DHA conversion is **~5% in men, ~10% in women**, which means 2 Tbsp ground flax (4.6 g ALA) yields maybe 200 mg EPA+DHA. Pregnant, lactating, or older adults should **supplement algae oil (250–500 mg EPA+DHA/day)**. Everyone else: I still recommend algae oil because it bypasses the conversion bottleneck.

faq.q: Is the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics position on vegan diets current?
faq.a: Yes — the **2016 Position Paper (Melina, Craig, Levin; J Acad Nutr Diet)** is still the most cited and current AND position. It states appropriately planned vegan diets are nutritionally adequate and appropriate for all life stages including pregnancy, infancy, childhood, adolescence, athletes, and older adults. **Appropriately planned** is the operative phrase — that's where this calculator and a real RD come in.

These are worked examples of a common lean-bulk method (which sets protein by bodyweight); the calculator above instead splits a calorie goal you enter into 20% protein / 25% fat / 55% carbs. Orientative only — adjust to your training volume and weekly weight trend, and consult a registered dietitian for a personalized plan.
